Over 90% of extremely preterm infants (born at less than 28 weeks of gestation) die within the first few days of life in low-income settings, compared to less than 10% in high-income settings (March of Dimes, 2012). 2. There remains uncertainty regarding the use of antenatal corticosteroids in pregnancies at later gestational ages. 3. This issue has gained importance due to the increasing number of cesarean sections performed at both term and late preterm gestations (McClure, 2007). 4. Neonates delivered via cesarean section are at an increased risk of respiratory complications, including respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) and transient tachypnea of the newborn (Hook, 1997; Maisels, 1977; Morrison, 1995). 5. The necessity of antenatal corticosteroids at term is debated, as only approximately 5% of these infants require admission for respiratory distress, and severe morbidity is rare (Stutchfield, 2005). 6. Concerns exist regarding the potential long-term adverse effects of corticosteroid exposure in more mature fetuses (Aiken, 2014; Steer, 2005). 7. As the risk of neonatal respiratory complications decreases with advancing gestational age (Morrison, 1995; Zanardo, 2004), delaying elective cesarean sections until 39 weeks or later appears to be an equally effective strategy (Al Kiaat, 2013; NICE, 2011; Stutchfield, 2005). 8. Antenatal corticosteroids are recommended by the World Health Organization as a priority intervention to prevent RDS and mortality in preterm infants (PMNCH, 2011; WHO, 2015). 9. However, the use of antenatal corticosteroids in lowand middle-income countries remains low (Vogel, 2014), suggesting an opportunity to improve outcomes for preterm infants through increased administration (Dalziel, 2014). 10. An analysis for the Global Action Report on Preterm Birth estimated that achieving universal coverage (95%) of antenatal corticosteroids in 75 priority countries by 2015 could have averted 373,000 additional infant deaths annually compared to 2010 figures (March of Dimes, 2012). 11. Caution has been advised in scaling up antenatal corticosteroid administration, particularly in low-income countries where access to other effective interventions, such as accurate pregnancy dating and neonatal resuscitation, may be limited (Lawn, 2013; Althabe, 2014). 12. A single course of antenatal corticosteroids has been identified as a highly effective and safe intervention for women at risk of preterm birth to reduce neonatal mortality and morbidity (Crowley, 1990; Roberts, 2006). 13. The benefits of antenatal corticosteroids were first described in a landmark trial conducted in New Zealand by Liggins and Howie in the late 1960s (Liggins, 1972). 14. Subsequent clinical trials and systematic reviews have confirmed the efficacy of antenatal corticosteroids in significantly reducing the risk of RDS, neonatal death, intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), and early sepsis (Crowley, 1990; Roberts, 2006). 15. Evidence suggests that in infants born more than seven days after antenatal corticosteroid treatment, there is no reduction in the incidence of RDS compared to those who did not receive antenatal corticosteroids (Roberts, 2006). 16. Repeat courses of antenatal corticosteroids have been administered to women who remain at risk of preterm birth seven or more days after an initial course. 17. Accumulating evidence has shown that repeat doses of the synthetic corticosteroid betamethasone are associated with a reduced risk of RDS and combined serious neonatal morbidity compared to a single course of antenatal corticosteroids (Crowther, 2015). 18. However, uncertainty persists regarding the effects of repeat antenatal corticosteroids on reduced birthweight and the long-term effects in both childhood and later life following repeated in utero exposure (Crowther, 2015). 19. Reassuringly, long-term follow-up of infants exposed to a single course of antenatal corticosteroids into early adulthood has not demonstrated an increased risk of cardio-metabolic disease (Dalziel, 2005; Dessens, 2000). Follow-up of infants up to early school age after repeat antenatal corticosteroid exposure has also been reassuring (Asztalos, 2010; Asztalos, 2013; Crowther, 2007; McKinlay, 2015; Peltonemi, 2009; Wapner, 2007). 20. The long-term effects of repeat corticosteroids on growth, the neuroendocrine system, and the risk of developing cardiovascular and metabolic disease in later life remain unknown (Crowther, 2015). 21. Antenatal corticosteroids have been administered prior to elective cesarean sections to minimize the risk of respiratory distress at late preterm and term gestations (Stutchfield, 2005; Tita, 2009). 22. Term infants born via cesarean section are at greater risk of respiratory morbidity, including transient tachypnea of the newborn and RDS, compared to term infants born vaginally (Hansen, 2008; Morrison, 1995; Sotiriadis, 2009). 23. There is limited data on the long-term effects of antenatal corticosteroid exposure prior to cesarean section at term. 24. The two main synthetic corticosteroids used in clinical practice are betamethasone and dexamethasone (NIH, 1994; PMNCH, 2011; RCOG, 2010; ACS CPG, 2015). 25. Despite widespread use, there is significant global variation in the type, preparation, dose, and method of administration of antenatal corticosteroids (Aleman, 2013; Erickson, 2001; Hui, 2007; Jobe, 2004; Parant, 2008; Pattanittum, 2008; Spencer, 2014; Vogel, 2014). 26. The optimal type of corticosteroid to use remains unclear (Brownfoot, 2013). 27. Both betamethasone and dexamethasone can cross the placenta in their biologically active forms and exert their effects with comparable efficiency (Jobe, 2004). 28. Intramuscular betamethasone can be administered in two different preparations: betamethasone sodium phosphate, which has a short half-life of six hours in maternal plasma, and betamethasone acetate, which has a longer half-life of approximately 12 hours (Ballard, 1975; Buckingham, 2006). 29. Liggins and Howie initially proposed that combining the two preparations of betamethasone would maximize drug efficacy (Liggins, 1972). 30. Antenatal corticosteroids have been administered in various ways, including orally (Egerman, 1998), intramuscularly (Liggins, 1972; Qublan, 2001; Shanks, 2010), intravenously (Petersen, 1983), intra-amniotically (Lefebvre, 1976; Murphy, 1982), and as a direct intramuscular injection to the fetus (Ljubic, 1999). 31. Betamethasone and dexamethasone, as antenatal corticosteroids, have been administered intramuscularly in a variety of regimens (Tables 1 and 2). 32. Trial regimens of a single course of antenatal betamethasone have included administering a total dose of betamethasone between 12 mg and 48 mg in single or multiple doses, at varied time intervals between doses (immediate, eight hours, 12 hours, and 24 hours), compared to no antenatal corticosteroids (Table 1). 33. Trial regimens of a single course of dexamethasone have included administering a total dose of dexamethasone between 20 mg and 24 mg in multiple divided doses, at varied time intervals between doses (eight hours, 12 hours, and 24 hours), compared to no antenatal corticosteroids (Table 2). 34. Trials have also compared the administration of repeat courses of antenatal corticosteroids to no repeat antenatal corticosteroids (Table 3). 35. Predominantly, these trials have administered betamethasone as the repeat course(s), apart from one trial that used dexamethasone (administered intramuscularly) as a repeat course (n = 31 participants) due to the temporary unavailability of betamethasone (Garite, 2009). 36.
